after.authors: Terada, M.; Yeh, T.; Natalia, H.; Baker, L. H.; Torres-Martinez, M.; Bolanle, D.; Shah, H.; Jiwani, U.; Zhang, L.; Park, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Background Since the World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed single-dose HPV vaccination in 2022, many countries have adopted this schedule. However, evidence regarding the schedule changes impact on HPV vaccination coverage remains limited. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, we assessed coverage changes following the schedule switch and explored stakeholders perspectives on factors influencing these trends. Methods Using WHO-UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage, we assessed first-dose HPV vaccination (HPV1) coverage among females in 49 countries that switched to a single-dose schedule during 2022-2024. We used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to compare mean HPV1 coverage before and after the switch, stratified by country and program characteristics. We also examined country-level changes in HPV1 and complete HPV vaccination (HPVc) coverage across all 49 countries. We then qualitatively interviewed 33 national and sub-national HPV vaccination stakeholders from 15 countries and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. Results Following the switch, significant increases in mean HPV1 coverage were observed among non-high-income countries (55.0% pre-switch vs. 63.3% post-switch, p=0.019), countries in the WHO African Region (58.9% vs. 71.6%, p=0.038), and programs employing school-based delivery (57.0% vs. 66.0%, p=0.010). Significant increases were also observed in programs targeting females only (56.3% vs. 65.9%, p=0.040), those targeting single-age cohorts (61.3% vs. 72.0%, p=0.013), and Gavi-supported countries (54.9% vs. 73.2%, p=0.010). Stakeholders attributed coverage trends to multiple factors beyond the schedule change, including recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions, concurrent programmatic changes, and broader contextual factors. Conclusion Although coverage trends varied across countries, improvement in HPV1 coverage in resource-limited settings suggested that the switch to a single-dose schedule may have facilitated recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions. Continued monitoring of vaccination coverage, implementation outcomes, and program sustainability is essential to understanding the long-term population-level implication of the single-dose recommendation.

after.abstract: Chronic tinnitus, the persistent perception of phantom sound, affects 14 to 15\% of adults yet lacks a validated neurophysiological biomarker, in part because group-average EEG analyses obscure the individual heterogeneity that defines the condition. In a multi-site case-control study of 544 participants (268 with tinnitus, mean age 45.4 {+/-} 16.1 years, 52\% female) across seven independent international sites, we applied normative modelling to quantify how far each person's resting-state EEG deviates from age- and hearing-adjusted healthy norms. Fusing spectral-power and connectivity deviations, a classifier detected tinnitus with an area under the curve of 0.832 under site-grouped cross-validation of precomputed normative features. The single most discriminative feature, rank-stable across all seven sites, was theta-band right orbitofrontal (pars orbitalis) connectivity, which dominated attribution by roughly an order of magnitude. Theta hyperconnectivity spanned frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks while primary auditory cortex showed negligible involvement, favouring failed top-down gating over bottom-up auditory overactivity. Features identifying tinnitus presence were orthogonal to symptom severity. These findings reframe chronic tinnitus as a frontoparietal attention-network disorder and nominate right orbitofrontal theta hyperconnectivity as a site-robust diagnostic feature. Data were collected within the TIDE project (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06520865).

after.authors: Mdingi, M. M.; Kullin, B.; Jung, H.; Gigi, R. M.; Babalola, C. M.; Medina-Marino, A. M.; Taylor, C. M.; Muzny, C.; Low, N.; Klausner, J. D.; Peters, R. P.
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Repeat Chlamydia trachomatis positivity after treatment may reflect persistent infection, reinfection, or residual nucleic acid. We compared paired ompA genotypes of C. trachomatis in pregnant women in South Africa and assessed macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Methods: We analyzed paired baseline and follow-up specimens from 43 pregnant women with C. trachomatis detected at two study visits. We determined ompA genotypes by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing and compared genotypes between visits. A fragment of the 23S rRNA gene was sequenced to identify selected macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Results: At baseline, ompA typing was successful in 38/43 (88%) specimens and 36/43 (84%) at follow-up, with paired genotype results available for 32 women (74%). Genotypes E, J and D predominated at baseline and follow-up. The same genotype was detected at both visits in 22/32 women (69%), whereas 10/32 (31%) had a different genotype at follow-up. Genotype concordance was observed in 2/2 (100%) women with paired results at the test-of-cure visit, 13/16 (81%) assessed at 32 weeks gestation, and 7/14 (50%) assessed postnatally. No targeted macrolide resistance associated mutations were detected in specimens with successful 23S rRNA sequencing. Conclusions: One-third of women with paired results had a different ompA genotype at follow-up, consistent with acquisition of a different strain after treatment. Concordant ompA genotypes may reflect persistence or reinfection with a strain sharing the same genotype, acquired from the same or a different partner. Macrolide resistance associated mutations were not detected. High-resolution typing methods would allow more detailed understanding of persistent C. trachomatis test positivity in this population.

after.title: Preprint: Smartphone-Based Assessment of Cognitive Variability in Alzheimer Disease
after.authors: Byun, A. J. S.
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Repeated smartphone testing can measure cognitive inconsistency that a single clinic visit cannot capture. We evaluated cognitive variability and everyday phone use in biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer disease (AD). METHODS: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment due to AD or mild AD dementia and cognitively unimpaired controls used Smartphone Monitoring Assessment in Real Time-Alzheimer (SMART-A) on their own phones. Response-time variability was adjusted for task demand and practice. RESULTS: Among 26 participants with cognitive data (14 controls, 12 AD), the four-marker variability composite was higher in AD (Hedges g = 1.29; 95% confidence interval, 0.53-2.06; P = .003) and correlated with baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment score (r = -0.60; P = .001). Memory-task accuracy was lower in AD at all four trials, and 64.5% versus 98.2% of sessions reached delayed recall (P < .001). Median phone-use bouts were shorter in AD (2.4 vs 5.4 minutes; P = .031), without a detectable pickup-frequency difference. Diary-reported bedtime was earlier in AD; sensor-derived sleep, activity, and mobility showed no statistically detectable differences. None of the 19 cross-domain contrasts survived false-discovery-rate correction. DISCUSSION: SMART-A supported repeated assessment over months in biomarker-confirmed AD. Cognitive variability, memory-task progression, and phone-use duration are promising complementary measures, requiring independent validation of reliability, incremental value, and sensitivity to clinical change.

after.title: Preprint: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
after.authors: Saboo, K. V.; Fan, J. M.; Tadayon, E.; Chang, E. F.; Rao, V. R.; Khambhati, A. N.
after.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

after.abstract: Distinguishing atypical from typical neurodevelopment requires large, well-characterized paediatric cohorts with harmonized multimodal neuroimaging and comprehensive phenotyping. Here, we describe the protocol for the Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (CPIP) Reference Sample, including the design, recruitment strategy, and phenotyping protocol, along with overviews of the imaging and genetics protocols. Using a multisite accelerated longitudinal design, we aim to recruit >800 participants aged 0 to 16 years at baseline, across three Canadian sites (Alberta Childrens Hospital, Calgary; The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Toronto; and CHU Sainte-Justine, Montreal) with comprehensive assessments at baseline and an annual follow-up, with additional follow-ups contingent on project extension. The protocol includes harmonized multimodal neuroimaging, extensive phenotyping across five broad domains: demographic, social and environmental factors; physical health and development; mental health and substance use; cognition; and temperament/personality, as well as DNA sequencing. Exclusion criteria are minimal to ensure a sample representative of the catchment areas of the participating hospitals. Data and protocols will be openly shared with the research community. The C-PIP Reference Sample will provide Canada's first large-scale pediatric neuroimaging reference cohort, enabling researchers to map typical and atypical trajectories from infancy through adolescence, identify biomarkers, examine genetic and contextual influences on brain development, and provide a normative comparison framework for clinical populations.

after.title: Preprint: Beyond billing codes: a proof-of-concept study of large language models for pregnancy episode reconstruction from clinical notes
after.authors: Schalkamp, A.-K.; Azzam, S.; Ayati, A.; Belov, A.; Wang, M.; Rudrapatna, V. A.
after.abstract: Background: Accurate identification of pregnancy episodes from electronic health records (EHRs) is essential for maternal and fetal health research. Existing approaches rely primarily on diagnosis and procedure codes, which may miss pregnancies documented outside the health system and are susceptible to coding errors. Clinical notes contain richer information but remain largely unexplored for this task. Objectives: To evaluate whether a large language model (LLM) can reconstruct complete pregnancy episodes directly from clinical notes. Methods: Chronologically concatenated notes and messages were provided to GPT-5, which identified episodes and extracted variables including assisted reproductive treatment, gestational age, outcome, and complications. Performance was benchmarked against manual chart review (gold standard) and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm in 30 patients comprising 74 pregnancies (20 patients in a held-out test set). Results: The LLM identified 53 of 54 test-set pregnancies versus 40/54 for a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm, with fewer spurious episodes (3 vs 24), corresponding to an F1 score for pregnancy detection against chart review of 0.96 vs 0.68. Among pregnancies identified by both methods, median absolute error was 0 vs 25.5 days for start dates (p<0.001) and 0 vs 1 day for end dates (p=0.044), and outcome accuracy was numerically but not significantly higher (0.84 vs 0.74 for exact outcome types; 0.92 vs 0.84 with abortion subtypes grouped). It additionally recovered information unavailable in structured data, including reproductive-treatment type and fetus-level outcomes. Conclusions: An LLM applied to clinical narratives identified pregnancy episodes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm while capturing richer clinical detail. Because the two approaches used different input data, these gains reflect both the information in clinical notes and the LLM itself. LLM-based extraction from clinical notes is a promising complement to code-based pregnancy phenotyping that warrants evaluation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts.

after.title: Preprint: Panel-agnostic tumour-only diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency
after.authors: Garcia-Lopez, D.; Hernando, B.; Chaves-Urbano, B.; Escobar-Rey, M.; Gomez-Sanchez, D.; Cadiz, A.; Gallego, A.; Mendiola, M.; Berjon, A.; Caleiras, E.; Garcia, J. F.; Hardisson, D.; Toledo, G.; Redondo, A.; Garcia, M. J.; Macintyre, G.
after.abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.

after.authors: Orcutt, X.; Nimgaonkar, V.; Chen, K.; Riaz, I.; Cohen, A.; Mamtani, R.; Gomes, M.; Long, Q.; Parikh, R. B.
after.abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

after.title: Preprint: CB-COMIL: interpretable prediction of melanoma immunotherapyresponse from multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images
after.authors: Rana, P.; Gide, T. N.; Adegoke, N.; Mao, Y.; N. Lo, S.; Berkovsky, S.; Coiera, E.; Long, G. V.; Wilmott, J. S.; Liu, S.
after.abstract: Deep learning models can predict melanoma immunotherapy response but rarely explain predictions biologically. Concept bottleneck models offer interpretable predictions, but have not been applied to multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and whether their learned concepts reproduce tissue measurements remains unclear. We developed CB-COMIL, which routes mIF predictions through four supervised concepts (immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index), decomposing each prediction exactly into concept contributions. Developed on 211 slides and evaluated on 42 slides from an independent, differently acquired test cohort, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020, 95% CI: -0.103 to 0.144). In 41 slides with complete measurements, learned concepts correlated with measured counterparts (Spearman: 0.61; 0.61-0.76), yet substituting measured values reduced macro-F1 from 0.68 to 0.48. CB-COMIL makes predictions interpretable without detectable performance loss, and our evaluation shows that concepts can faithfully determine predictions without reproducing the corresponding biological measurements.

after.authors: Park, D.-W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Casey Eye Institute, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon, USA
after.abstract: Objective To examine wearable heart rate measures in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), reporting an exploratory observation in neovascular AMD. Results This cross-sectional All of Us analysis used minute-level Fitbit heart rate from adults aged [≥]50 years with eye care records. Among the 55 participants with neovascular AMD, the mean date of complete Fitbit recording days fell a median of 1.9 years after the first neovascular AMD diagnosis code. The 7259 comparators had no AMD. The planned primary test, sleeping heart rate with any AMD, was not statistically significant (odds ratio [OR] per 10 beats/min, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.97-1.29). Higher standard deviation of 5-minute average beat intervals (SDANN), a secondary measure, was associated with higher odds of neovascular AMD versus no AMD (OR per 10 ms, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.04-1.21], uncorrected P = 0.002, Bonferroni-adjusted P = 0.051 for 22 comparisons). In an exploratory comparison with non-neovascular AMD, the OR was 1.20 (95% CI, 1.08-1.32). After 24-hour heart rate adjustment, the OR versus no AMD was 1.13 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24). No associations were detected for epiretinal membrane or cataract. This exploratory observation warrants testing in recordings preceding conversion.

after.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss, with a significant impact on the elderly population worldwide. Machine learning and deep learning methods, combined with optical coherence tomography (OCT), are promising for the rapid diagnosis of AMD. However, most models focus only on one single OCT imaging modality or neglect clinical information. To improve this problem, we design a deep multimodal framework that integrates OCT images with clinical text data for the detection of AMD. Then, we evaluate the proposed model using metrics, such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F-score, and the area under the curve (AUC), achieving excellent detection results at both the image level and patient level. Next, we conduct computational efficiency analysis and independent external validation to further demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed model.In addition,we provide visualization results with explainable AI technique to further show the effectiveness of the proposed model. Our proposed model using multimodal strategy involving machine learning along with available clinical text and OCT imaging data accurately predicts individuals with AMD. Therefore, the use of machine learning and explainable AI in AMD detection may ultimately improve early diagnosis and offer more precise and personalized treatment strategies, improving the management ofAMD and preservingvision.

after.authors: Ragosta, A.; Bruni, F.
after.abstract: Objective: To determine whether executable encodings of three ocular hypertension guidelines, produced under a prospectively frozen pipeline barring author-defined operationalisations, are judged faithful by independent clinical review before execution, and to characterise findings on retained content, exclusions and divisions. Methods: Under a registered protocol, one ophthalmologist encoded European Glaucoma Society (EGS), American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines; a second encoded a sample. A gate barred author-defined operationalisations. Before execution, two other ophthalmologists reviewed branches, exclusions and division records against predefined materiality criteria. Results: The gate admitted 0, 2 and 1 branches (EGS, AAO, NICE) from 748, 322 and 198 eligible units. Review of these branches raised no primary finding (AAO 0/2, NICE 0/1); at these denominators, uninformative. In the overlap, one NICE omission (laser trabeculoplasty) was judged material. The exclusion reviewer flagged material source-stated decision content in 601/2,109, 216/234 and 151/179 excluded passages. A masked post-hoc reader agreed with 31/50, 11/50 and 28/50 sampled flags; he judged 1/246 passages directly relevant to the initial treat-or-observe decision and 0/100, 0/68 and 8/78 needed to preserve a retained unit's meaning. No synthetic case resolved to observation. Conclusion: Without author-defined choices, few branches were instantiable and none resolved to observation. Fidelity was not determinable at these denominators; exclusion flags were reader-dependent, and some NICE exclusions may have carried meaning needed by retained units. Exclusion review shows what a scope restriction sets aside; its reproducibility must be established before it measures fidelity.

after.authors: Serigatto, H. R.; Kokitsu-Nakata, N. M.; Vendramini-Pittoli, S.; Tonello, C.; Passos-Bueno, M. R.; Zechi-Ceide, R. M.
after.abstract: The oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome is a rare condition characterized by ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, mandibular hypoplasia, preauricular tags, and ear anomalies. Despite presenting a clinically recognizable pattern defined by the overlap of craniofacial microsomia and frontonasal dysplasia, its etiology remains unknown. Males and females are equally affected, and there is no recurrence reported. Genetic investigations performed to date could not clarify this issue yet. To further investigate Mendelian inheritance and test the hypothesis of a possible monogenic cause, we performed exome sequencing in a case series of Brazilian individuals from a single center with the clinical diagnosis of oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome, including both solo and trio-based exome sequencing. The results provided here further support a non-traditional inheritance model, requiring additional studies including multi-omics approaches to elucidate its etiology.

after.title: Preprint: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
after.authors: Petrovska, J.; Rubio-Aliaga, I.; T'Sjoen, D.; Van Wynsberghe, J.; Vanakker, O.; Munch, J.; Cabello, E. M.; Bonny, O.; Wagner, C. A.; Bachmann-Gagescu, R.
after.abstract: Background: The majority of rare diseases are caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene with Mendelian inheritance. In contrast, common diseases typically have complex genetic etiology, ranging from a cumulative impact of many common genetic variants with small individual effects, to fewer rare variants with larger effects, with monogenic forms at the rare end of the spectrum. While unknown prevalence of the monogenic fraction of common diseases and incomplete penetrance make identification of such monogenic forms of common diseases particularly challenging, their diagnosis can be essential for precision medicine. Automated rare variant prioritization tools, such as Exomiser, aid whole exome sequencing-based rare genetic disease diagnostics. However, Exomiser's utility has not been systematically assessed in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases prior to this study. Methods: We evaluated and optimized Exomiser for prioritization of rare pathogenic variants in common disease using a large kidney stone disease (KSD) cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). First, we benchmarked Exomiser's performance across different settings for KSD "gold standard" variants in established KSD genes with Mendelian inheritance. Next, we utilized the optimal pipeline for discovery of novel KSD genes and compared Exomiser's findings with results from gene-level rare variant enrichment analyses in an extended in-house cohort and the UK Biobank. Results: With the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all (94%, N = 48) previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated 62 novel genes predominantly involved in ion homeostasis, which are now available to the scientific community as candidate genes for KSD. Out of these genes, orthogonal approaches also support ABCC6 as a strong KSD risk gene, in line with previous research, providing a proof-of-principle supporting the utility of Exomiser in the context of common disease. Conclusions: This study serves as an example for automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases, which is a key step for precision medicine.

after.title: Preprint: Additional Vascular Imaging in Women With Acute Cerebral Ischemia: Thresholds for Cost-Effectiveness
after.authors: Boettger, P.; Klug, J.; Agarwal, A.; Alhaj Omar, O.; Juenemann, M.; Buerke, M.; Sossalla, S.; Carrera, E.
after.abstract: Background: Women with acute cerebral ischemia receive intracranial vascular imaging less often than men, but the value of expanding imaging is uncertain. We estimated the treatment rates and functional benefits required for additional imaging to be cost-effective. Methods: We developed a decision tree and state-transition model comparing additional imaging followed by timely endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for M1 occlusion with current care from Ontario public-payer and US Medicare perspectives. Women-specific 90-day modified Rankin Scale distributions from HERMES were projected over a lifetime. We jointly varied the proportion of additional scans leading to additional timely EVT and the treatment effect relative to HERMES. Cost-effectiveness thresholds were CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. Program costs represented health-care resources in Ontario and additional payments under Medicare. Results: At variable program costs of CAD 1,000 or USD 1,000 per additional scan, assuming the full HERMES effect and no additional fixed costs or pathway-related harm, expected cost-effectiveness required one additional timely EVT per 48 scans in Ontario and 57 under Medicare (2.07% and 1.74%, respectively). Treatment rates of 3.07% and 2.65% were required for a 90% probability of cost-effectiveness under these assumptions. At three additional thrombectomies per 100 scans and the same costs, treatment effects had to reach 76.9% and 67.3% of the HERMES effect. With the full effect, 1,000 additional scans at this treatment rate yielded approximately 5 additional functionally independent survivors at 90 days. Deterministic analyses restricted to 5 years increased the required treatment rates to 4.44% and 4.22%. Conclusions: Additional vascular imaging in women could be cost-effective when a small proportion of scans leads to timely thrombectomy, provided sufficient functional benefit is retained. Prospective evaluations should assess additional treatment opportunities, functional outcomes and program costs against these conditional thresholds, which depend on projected long-term outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Asking Conversational Artificial Intelligence about Health and Subsequent Actions among Adults in Japan: A Cross-sectional Web Survey
after.authors: Ichikawa, M.
after.abstract: Introduction: People increasingly ask conversational artificial intelligence (AI) about health; however, how this relates to care seeking in Japan, where universal health coverage renders care accessible, remains unknown. This study described how many adults ask AI about health, why and when, what they do afterward, and how much they trust AI compared with other sources. Methods: This two-stage cross-sectional survey employed a commercial web panel (October-November 2026). A screening survey of adults aged [≥]20 years (10,000 responses; 8,209 analyzed) estimated prevalence. A main survey of users (1,000 responses; 735 analyzed) asked about purposes, the most recent use and subsequent actions, and trust in seven information sources. Responses were weighted by sex and age. Results: In the past 6 months, 40.3% of adults (95% confidence interval, 39.3-41.4) asked conversational AI about health. The most recent use occurred before a medical visit for 39.0%, after a visit for 23.4%, and when no visit was being considered for 37.6%. Subsequently, 35.4% visited a medical facility; 12.8% (10.3-15.3) decided not to visit or postponed a visit (5.1% of all adults). Forgoing or delaying was more frequent among users with high trust in AI (trusting it completely or a lot; 22.5% vs. 10.9% among others). Among pre-visit users, it was less frequent with high trust in health professionals (16.7% vs. 30.9%) and did not clearly differ by trust in AI. Of users, 61.4% had high trust in health professionals and 14.3% in AI. Conclusions: In Japan, approximately 4 in 10 adults asked AI about health, and 1 in 8 users forwent or delayed a visit. This was more common with high trust in AI; among pre-visit users, it was associated with low trust in health professionals. How trust in AI and health professionals relates to care seeking warrants further study.

after.title: Preprint: Task-specific fine-tuning versus frontier large language models for RoB 2 risk of bias assessment: development and external benchmark evaluation of RoB-BERT
after.authors: Pitre, T.; Mah, J.; Azlan, A.; Nguyen, D.; Zeraatkar, D.; Agarwal, A.; Guyatt, G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University Health Network and University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada
after.abstract: Background: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to assess risk of bias in randomized trials, but how task-specific fine-tuned models compare with frontier models remains uncertain. Objective: To develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. Methods: RoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. Results: In ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% ({kappa} 0.35) and 53.5% ({kappa} 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% ({kappa} 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% ({kappa} 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% ({kappa} 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% ({kappa} 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% ({kappa} 0.16), 47.3% ({kappa} 0.17), 31.0% ({kappa} 0.03) and 46.5% ({kappa} 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%. On the 52 ROBoto2 trials rated by two assessors, the second assessor's sensitivity for the reference assessor's high-risk domains was 23.1% (specificity 90.3%) and RoB-BERT's was 30.8% (specificity 92.7%). RoB-BERT located 95.7% of its quotations verbatim in the report and cost US$0.005 per trial, 2% to 6% of the frontier models' cost. Conclusions: RoB-BERT agreed with single human assessors at least as closely as two human assessors agreed with each other, and matched or exceeded frontier LLMs at a fraction of their cost. The results show the poor reliability of human assessors using RoB 2 and the need for consensus ratings, with RoB-BERT potentially serving as one rater.

items.title: Preprint: Longitudinal Trends in Secondary Cardiovascular Prevention After Peripheral Artery Disease Diagnosis

after.title: Preprint: Longitudinal Trends in Secondary Cardiovascular Prevention After Peripheral Artery Disease Diagnosis
after.authors: Kallis, K.; Kumar, P.; Kang-Sim, E.; Neels, N.; Deng, J.; Quitevis, C. R.; Alsaigh, T.; Ross, E. G.
after.abstract: Background: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is associated with substantial cardiovascular and limb-related morbidity, making long-term cardiovascular prevention an important part of care. However, longitudinal patterns of guideline-based quality measure achievement after PAD diagnosis remain poorly characterized in broad clinical populations. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Epic Cosmos electronic health record (EHR) data to identify adults aged 18 to 75 years with PAD diagnosed from 2019 to 2023. Four cardiovascular prevention components based on Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Quality Measures were assessed annually after PAD diagnosis: blood pressure target achievement, documented tobacco-free status, antiplatelet therapy, and statin therapy. Complete achievement was defined as meeting all four measures. We assessed quality-measure achievement across groups, three-year quality-index trends, and associations between complete achievement and subsequent outcomes. Results: Among 906,686 patients, model-adjusted first-year achievement was 60.6% for tobacco-free status, 61.9% for blood pressure control, 39.5% for antiplatelet therapy, and 63.4% for statin therapy; 10.4% achieved all four. Model-adjusted complete achievement was 12.4% in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), 10.5% in claudication, and 10.2% in unspecified PAD. Model-adjusted rates varied by sex, race/ethnicity, insurance type, rurality, PAD severity, and comorbidities and ranged from 7.6% to 14.7%. Complete achievement in year 1 was associated with lower adjusted odds of amputation (odds ratio (OR), 0.91), vascular procedures (OR, 0.86), stroke (OR, 0.90), and myocardial infarction (OR, 0.94). Conclusions: In this large national EHR cohort, individual quality measures improved after PAD diagnosis, but only 10.4% of patients achieved all four assessed components during the first year after diagnosis. Differences across quality domains and patient subgroups highlight variation in longitudinal cardiovascular risk prevention, particularly among patients with less clinically apparent disease.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Evaluation of a Brief Educational Intervention to Improve Healthcare Provider Communication About Autism Genetic Testing

after.title: Preprint: Evaluation of a Brief Educational Intervention to Improve Healthcare Provider Communication About Autism Genetic Testing
after.authors: Pilson, O. G.; Barna, L. S.; Grimes, T.; Salako, T. A.; Ramirez-Renta, G. M.; Wang, A.; Gunter, C.
after.abstract: Although professional guidelines recommend offering genetic testing following an autism diagnosis, uptake remains low in the United States. Healthcare providers frequently report limited education and uncertainty discussing autism genetics with patients and families. We developed and evaluated a brief educational intervention to improve provider communication about autism genetic testing, consisting of animated videos addressing autism genetics, available testing options, and strategies for discussing testing with autistic individuals and families. We evaluated the intervention among 100 U.S.-based healthcare providers and a community panel of 99 autistic adults. Participants completed a validated measure of genetic literacy before viewing the videos, then evaluated the intervention and its perceived impact on genetic testing. Providers showed higher genetic literacy than the general U.S. population, yet only 23% reported frequently discussing genetic testing before the intervention. Afterward, 86% reported greater likelihood of recommending genetic testing following diagnosis, and 88% reported the videos changed how they would discuss genetics with patients and families. Both cohorts rated the resources favorably, and 71% of autistic adults reported greater likelihood of pursuing genetic testing after viewing the videos. Brief, communication-focused educational resources may improve workflows for autism genetic testing and support informed decision-making for providers, autistic individuals, and their families.

after.title: Preprint: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
after.authors: Dragostinov, Y.; Hsu, R. E.; Ennis, G. W.; Londono-Correa, D.; Schwaba, T.; Nivard, M. G.; Tucker-Drob, E. M.
after.abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

after.title: Preprint: Escape from X-chromosome inactivation increases disease risk and drives sex-differential genetic effects: a population-scale PheXWAS
after.authors: Perez-Elena, M. A.; Salvoro, C.; Matias, D.; Satari, L.; Puiggros, M.; Zugasti, D.; Alonso-Parrilla, L.; Torrents, D.
after.abstract: X chromosome (Xchr) contribution to complex traits remains incomplete, due to its unique inheritance pattern and its inactivation mechanism. Therefore, we gathered data from 800,000 individuals from the UK Biobank and dbGaP, and performed a sex-stratified phenome-wide association study of Xchr variation across 3,741 complex traits. Heritability analyses revealed sex-specific patterns and an overall involvement of Xchr in complex phenotypes. We identified 6,531 loci significantly associated with 402 complex traits, with a higher proportion of associations consistent with dominant inheritance than observed for autosomes. Although effect directions were largely concordant between sexes, loci with significant effect-size differences were enriched for escape-gene associations. Escape genes were depleted among trait-associated loci and strongly enriched for risky disease effects. These association patterns enabled prediction of escape status for unannotated genes. This overview of Xchr contribution to complex traits suggests inactivation escape as a clear risky feature for females.

after.title: Preprint: Transcriptional aging across CNS tissues in the ALS-FTD spectrum reflects clock architecture and disease-associated cellular signatures
after.authors: Zhao, T.; Wu, G.; Hoffman, M. M.; Belzil, V. V.
after.abstract: Background. We examined transcriptomic (gene expression-based) aging in postmortem central nervous system (CNS) tissues from donors across the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum and investigated the molecular and cellular features underlying disease-associated differences in transcriptional aging clocks. Methods. Six transcriptomic clocks (RNAAgeCalc DESeq2, GTExAge, Pearson and GenAge; Pasta REG and age-shift) were applied to 2,235 RNA-sequencing samples from 609 donors across 11 CNS regions, with adjustment for age and tissue-specific technical variables. We compared transcriptional age across ALS, ALS-FTD, FTD, and controls, examining regional variation, gene-level contributions, cell composition, disease duration, and C9orf72 status, with independent validation of gene contributions in a cervical spinal cord cohort. Results. Disease-associated differences in transcriptional age varied by diagnosis, tissue, and clock. ALS and ALS-FTD showed the strongest differences in spinal cord, while FTD differences localized primarily to the frontal and temporal cortex. In ALS spinal cord, RNAAgeCalc DESeq2 estimates were lower than controls, whereas other clocks estimated higher transcriptional age when significant. CHIT1 was identified as the primary contributor to the DESeq2 transcriptional age decrease in ALS. Cell composition adjustment attenuated ALS spinal cord differences, reflecting microglial, lymphocyte, oligodendrocyte, and astrocyte signatures, though the lumbar GenAge increase in transcriptional age and DESeq2 decrease remained significant. The higher transcriptional age in ALS motor cortex also remained significantafter adjustment. Clinical associations were likewise clock dependent. Higher spinal DESeq2 age acceleration (AA) was associated with longer ALS duration, though this association was strongly influenced by the CHIT1 term. Higher GTExAge AA in cervical spinal cord, thoracic spinal cord, and occipital cortex was associated with shorter disease duration; no significant associations were observed for the other clock-tissue combinations or for ALS-FTD. No clock differed by C9orf72 repeat expansion status. Conclusions. In this study we found disease-associated differences in transcriptional age that localize to clinically relevant tissues. Differences in transcriptional aging across the ALS-FTD spectrum reflect interactions among clock architecture, disease-associated gene expression, tissue region, and cellular composition. Resolving these components reveals the biological context underlying divergent clock estimates and provides a framework for interpreting changes in transcriptional aging.

after.title: Preprint: Unified Machine Learning Model for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Frailty, and Fall Risk Using Multimodal Motor-Function Data
after.authors: Akter, S.; Guess, T.; Sarker, S.; Hockett, S. A.; Kiselica, A.; Hall, J.; Rao, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, United States
after.abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. Objective: This study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. Methods: Community-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. Results: With class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The final extra trees model achieved a mean AUC of 0.645 (95% CI 0.569-0.722); discrimination was best for MCI (AUC 0.779, 95% CI 0.680-0.872) and lower for frailty (0.606) and fall risk (0.551). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. Learning curves suggested that fall-risk prediction would benefit from more participants. Conclusions: A unified model predicted MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from one sensor-based assessment and performed as well as 3 separate models. It identified motor features shared across the conditions and used the link between frailty and fall risk. It performed best for MCI; with improvement for frailty and fall risk, recalibration, and external validation, such a model could support efficient screening of older adults for several conditions at once. KEYWORDS mild cognitive impairment; frailty; fall risk; machine learning; multi-label classification; classifier chain; gait; dual task; explainable artificial intelligence; Shapley additive explanations.

after.title: Preprint: Germline Variant Profiling of NA12878 Chromosome 22 Identifies the Loss-of-Function CYP2D6*3 and *4 Pharmacogenetic Alleles
after.authors: Mallick, S.; Singh, B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Biotecnika Info Labs Pvt Ltd., Bangalore, India
after.abstract: The approach used in this project to call germline variants from short-read sequencing data forms the basis of a great deal of current human genetics, whether it be in population studies or in diagnostic testing. A full germline variant-calling workflow according to the GATK Best Practices was constructed and carried out using public whole-genome sequencing data from the reference sample NA12878. In order to comply with the limitations of a laptop (an Intel Core i3, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu via WSL2), the analysis was limited to chromosome 22. The reads for chromosome 22 were streamed directly from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage CRAM file (run ERR3239334), converted into paired FASTQ files, checked using FastQC and MultiQC, and then cleaned with fastp. The cleaned reads were aligned to a GRCh38 reference containing only chromosome 22 using BWA-MEM, after which they were sorted, duplicates were marked and the base quality scores were recalibrated before variants were called with GATK HaplotypeCaller. The GATK-recommended hard filters were applied separately to SNPs and indels, and the variants that passed these filters were annotated using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) and summarised with a Python script. From the 81,599 raw calls, 73,570 (90.2%) survived the filtering process, and the transition/transversion ratio for the SNPs that passed filtering was 2.04. Of the annotated variant alleles, 98.9% were already present in the catalogue, 734 affected the coding sequence in 270 genes, and no variant corresponded to a pathogenic entry in ClinVar. Examination using IGV verified the read support for the selected high-impact calls, including the variants that define the CYP2D6*3 and *4 alleles, consistent with the published genotype of NA12878. The main limitations were a reduced effective depth of 8.6x, resulting from an incomplete read-collation step which retained about 31% of the read pairs, and the use of a chromosome-only reference.

items.title: Preprint: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data

after.title: Preprint: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
after.authors: Gutierrez-Alvarez, I.; Rojas, A.; Calzadilla-Bertot, L.; Dopazo, J.; Romero-Gomez, M.; Loucera, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, Barcelona, Spain
after.abstract: Background. Short-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. Methods. From a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings. 771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores' high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 g/L, platelets below 150 x10^9/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. Interpretation. An interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death.

after.title: Preprint: What Does an Agent-Run Clinic Cost? Protocol for a Prospective Observational Study of the Compute Cost of Completed Work in a Clinical Agent Fleet
after.authors: Elalfy, O.; Youssef, S.; Davids, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Wai Health Inc, Palo Alto, CA, United States; The London Wellness Clinic Ltd, London, United Kingdom
after.abstract: Background: Decisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. Objective: This study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. Conclusions: The compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial Registration: None. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study.
